prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings place B019 first, and I agree on the merits and not because the support is unanimous. The chain runs from the incretin effect and proglucagon processing, through identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and its insulinotropic and satiety actions in humans, to drugs with confirmed glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal effects in large independent trials. It is physiological discovery in the classical sense, with an unusually complete line to patient benefit and a stable interpretation after many years of use. Holst (human physiology and secretion), Drucker (proglucagon-derived peptide and receptor biology and translation) and Mojsov (the active peptide) are the three scientific contributions I can most clearly separate and defend.
statement.case_against: The credit is the weak point. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested, and the supplied list omits others, Habener being the one colleagues repeatedly name, so a three-person prize will look incomplete to some. Leaving out Knudsen means not crediting the long-acting analogue design that turned the physiology into semaglutide and liraglutide, which is a real cost if the committee thinks the drug step belongs in the prize. Long-term safety and outcome data are still accumulating, though not enough to argue for delay.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen and omits Mojsov, treating her role in identifying the active peptide as real but secondary to the drug-design step.
responses.response: I take the point that Knudsen's acylated analogues are what reached patients, and I will not call her contribution minor. But the prize is for a discovery, and the discovery is the physiology and the identity of the active hormone. Dropping Mojsov removes the one contributor who ties the peptide's identity to its biological activity, while keeping a company scientist whose work is optimisation of an already-defined principle. If the committee wants the translational step credited, a more principled route is to ask whether a second part is warranted. Swapping Knudsen for Mojsov inside one part is not that. I stay with Mojsov and remain open to being persuaded on how the translational credit is handled.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks B040 third and would credit Hall alone, setting Sabatini and Schreiber aside because of unresolved credit and conduct questions.
responses.response: I agree that a Hall-only configuration is the cleanest for TOR, since Hall identified TOR and defined its role in growth control, and this avoids a difficult allocation. My hesitation is not the credit but the weight. TOR is fundamental and mature, but its therapeutic yield through rapalogs is more modest than the conceptual claim, and I rank it below candidates with clearer physiological and clinical reach. I would not oppose it as a one-person prize if the committee wants a basic-science element, but I do not think it should displace B019 or work to dilute it.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks B014 third with only June and Sadelain, noting that Rosenberg's adoptive cell therapy and Eshhar's earlier chimeric receptor concept complicate credit.
responses.response: This is a serious qualification, and I made the same observation in my own opening. I included Rosenberg because adoptive cell transfer and early gene-modified T-cell trials are the framework June and Sadelain worked in, but a two-person prize is easier to defend than three if Eshhar cannot be credited. I would not call CAR-T a weaker discovery than incretins. Its attribution is simply harder to resolve cleanly with the supplied names, so I keep it as an alternative and not as my preferred prize.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks B016 fourth, noting that six names cannot fit and that a trio must choose between channelrhodopsin discovery and neuronal application, and ranks B020 (imatinib) sixth.
responses.response: I agree that optogenetics is the most contested allocation on the list. Nagel and Hegemann (with Bamberg) identified channelrhodopsin, and Deisseroth, Boyden and Miesenböck contributed the neuronal and genetic-targeting side, so any three will exclude strong claimants. I use optogenetics routinely as a circuit tool, which is a reason to be careful: familiarity with its usefulness is not evidence that the credit is settled. I still regard the method as an exceptional discovery, which is why it stays as my first alternative, but the difficulty of drawing the line is a real reason not to put it ahead of B019.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks TNF blockade (B032) third, arguing that Feldmann and Maini form a coherent bench-to-bedside pair and that the concept chain from synovial cytokine biology to clinical proof is clear.
responses.response: I find the Feldmann and Maini pairing attractive on attribution, because two people and a clear concept is the opposite of the incretin credit problem. My doubt is about timing and about the strength of the original discovery. The scientific step is the demonstration that TNF is a dominant driver and can be blocked in rheumatoid arthritis, and it has been recognised over a long time. It is also less original than the physiology behind GLP-1. I do not rule it out, but I would not choose it over B019, B014 or B016 for the prize.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is strong enough, relative to the physiological work and to Habener (not on the supplied list), to justify a place among three
Whether the committee wants to credit drug development (Knudsen) in the same part or in a separate part, which would have to respect the three-person limit on the union of laureates
Whether the supplied credit names are sufficient to reflect the history of GLP-1 or whether the case is better deferred until a fuller review of priority is done
How much weight to give clinical outcome data still accumulating for cardiovascular, renal and long-term safety endpoints
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My profile documents no co-authorship or other tie to any credited name on the shortlist. My documented connections (Grillner, Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann) do not involve the incretin candidates, and my motor-circuit work only touches optogenetics as a user of the method, so I do not see that as requiring recusal.
